questions.stem: Which Article of the Indian Constitution deals with National Emergency?
questions.explanation: Art 352 — National Emergency, can be proclaimed on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion. Art 356 — President's Rule in a state (State Emergency). Art 360 — Financial Emergency (never invoked). Art 368 deals with the procedure for constitutional amendments.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: How many times has a National Emergency been proclaimed in India so far?
questions.explanation: National Emergency has been declared three times: 1962 (China war), 1971 (Pakistan war / Bangladesh liberation), and 1975-77 (the 'Internal Emergency' on grounds of internal disturbance, imposed by Indira Gandhi). Only the third was for an internal cause; the 44th Amendment, 1978, replaced 'internal disturbance' with the stricter 'armed rebellion' to prevent a repeat.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 356, popularly called 'President's Rule', relates to a failure of constitutional machinery in:
questions.explanation: Art 356 — when a state government cannot be run according to the Constitution, the President (on the Governor's report) may assume executive powers of the state. State legislative powers are transferred to Parliament. Maximum duration: 6 months at a time, extendable up to 3 years with parliamentary approval. Frequently litigated — S. R. Bommai (1994) laid down judicial-review guidelines.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Financial Emergency under Article 360 has been proclaimed in India:
questions.explanation: Art 360 — Financial Emergency — has never been invoked, even during the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis. If declared, the Union can direct states on financial matters, reduce the salaries of state employees and even judges, and reserve all state money bills for the President's assent. The 1991 crisis was handled through IMF assistance and the opening-up reforms, not via Art 360.

questions.stem: During a National Emergency, most Fundamental Rights can be suspended — but which rights are protected under Article 20 and Article 21 and cannot be suspended?

options.option_text: Protection in conviction and right to life/liberty

questions.explanation: The 44th Amendment (1978) guarantees that Art 20 (protection against retrospective criminal laws, double jeopardy, self-incrimination) and Art 21 (right to life and personal liberty) can never be suspended, even during a National Emergency. Before 1978 all Fundamental Rights could be suspended. The right to property was removed from the list of FRs in 1978 and is now a legal right under Art 300A.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: A Proclamation of National Emergency must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within:
questions.explanation: Post-44th Amendment — a National Emergency proclamation must be approved within 1 month of issue by both Houses with a special majority (majority of total membership plus 2/3 of members present and voting). Earlier it was 2 months with a simple majority. Once approved it continues for 6 months at a time; Lok Sabha can revoke it by simple majority any time.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) replaced which phrase in Article 352?
questions.explanation: The 44th Amendment, brought by the Janata government after the 1975-77 Emergency, tightened Art 352 so that vague 'internal disturbance' could no longer be used as a ground — it has to be the much higher bar of 'armed rebellion'. The Amendment also required the Cabinet's written recommendation (not just the PM's), and made judicial review of the proclamation possible.
